final_answer:
Let
\[
P(x)=\prod_{m\ge3,\ m\text{ odd}}R_m(x)^{a_m}.
\]
The identity \(P(x)P(-x)=P(x^2-2)\), together with \(P(0)=\pm1\), forces this form: roots must be finite backward-invariant under \(x\mapsto x^2-2\), hence are \(2\cos(2\pi k/m)\) with \(m\) odd.

For \(R_m\), the cubic map satisfies
\[
y^3-3y=2\cos(3\theta)\quad\text{when }y=2\cos\theta.
\]
Thus the resultant equation gives the exponent relations
\[
a_3=3,\qquad a_9=1,\qquad a_{27}=a_{81}=\cdots=0,
\]
and every \(a_m=0\) for \(v_3(m)=1\), \(m>3\). All remaining possible factors have \(3\nmid m\).

Now
\[
R_m(2)=(-1)^{\varphi(m)/2}\Phi_m(1),
\]
where \(\Phi_m(1)=p\) if \(m\) is a power of the prime \(p\), and \(1\) otherwise. Since
\[
R_3(2)^3R_9(2)=(-3)^3(-3)=81,
\]
the remaining factors must contribute
\[
\frac{-2835}{81}=-35.
\]
Also
\[
\frac{R_m'(2)}{R_m(2)}=\frac{J_2(m)}{24},
\]
so after \(R_3^3R_9\), whose logarithmic derivative contribution is \(4\), the remaining factors must have degree \(37\) and logarithmic derivative \(195\).

The only prime-power contributions compatible with \(-35\) are one \(5\)-power and one \(7\)-power. Checking the degree and derivative constraints leaves the unique choice
\[
R_7,\quad R_{25},\quad R_{65}.
\]
Indeed
\[
\deg(R_7R_{25}R_{65})=3+10+24=37
\]
and
\[
\frac{J_2(7)+J_2(25)+J_2(65)}{24}
=2+25+168=195.
\]

Therefore
\[
\boxed{P(x)=R_3(x)^3R_7(x)R_9(x)R_{25}(x)R_{65}(x)}.
\]
